property_summary: The reference contract only accepts calls with exactly 10 ether, while the mutant accepts calls with exactly 1 ether, breaking the 10-ether-only acceptance rule.
For any call with value exactly 10 ether, c.balance must increase by that amount modulo the self-destruct path; the mutant rejects 10 ether and fails this rule.

The fallback function must only proceed when block.timestamp is strictly greater than pastBlockTime; the mutant's >= allows duplicate timestamps, enabling a second call with the same timestamp to succeed instead of reverting.
For any valid timestamp, a second call with the same timestamp must always revert; the bug allows it to succeed.

After any sequence of valid fallback calls, if a call with a given block.timestamp succeeds, then pastBlockTime must be strictly greater than that timestamp; the bug's >= allows pastBlockTime to equal the timestamp, violating this invariant.

After a successful call, the stored pastBlockTime must always be strictly greater than the timestamp of any previously successful call; the bug allows a later call at the same timestamp to succeed, leaving pastBlockTime equal to its own timestamp.
For any call where block.number % 15 != 0, the contract's Ether balance must not decrease; the buggy version allows a decrease when block.number % 10 == 0 and block.number % 15 != 0.

After any sequence of calls to fallback with exactly 10 ether, the contract's balance should always be either zero (sent to msg.sender on a qualifying block) or remain unchanged, never transferred to a fixed address.

After any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether, if the transfer condition (block.number % 15 == 0) is met, the entire contract balance must be transferred to msg.sender; the mutant instead transfers to address(0x0), breaking this invariant.

After any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether, when block.number % 15 == 0, the entire balance must leave the contract; the buggy version sends it to address(0x0) instead of msg.sender, so the subsequent balance of the original caller remains 0 while the contract's balance becomes 0.
After any call to fallback, the contract's balance changes by exactly msg.value, but the bug allows calls with any msg.value causing a mismatch.

For any call to fallback with msg.value > 0 and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the correct contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp, but the buggy version skips this update when the first require (msg.value == 10 ether) is removed, causing pastBlockTime to remain stale after calls with insufficient value.

For any call to the fallback with any value, if it succeeds then the contract's pastBlockTime must be updated to the current block timestamp; the buggy version allows a successful call with msg.value < 10 ether that does NOT update pastBlockTime because the first require was removed and the second require's check on block.timestamp may either revert or fall through without updating the storage when the call itself was empty of execution.
For any call to fallback with msg.value != 10 ether, the transaction must revert; the buggy version allows calls with msg.value != 10 ether to succeed, changing the revert outcome.

For any call to fallback with any value, if the transaction does not revert, then the pastBlockTime must equal block.timestamp; the buggy version allows a non-reverting call with insufficient ether that does not update pastBlockTime, breaking the invariant.

For any sequence of admissible calls to fallback, the contract's pastBlockTime must always strictly increase from its previous value. The mutant removes the block.timestamp > pastBlockTime check, allowing calls in the same block to leave pastBlockTime unchanged.

For any two admissible fallback calls in the same block, the reference contract's balance cannot decrease by more than the first call's locked Ether, while the mutant allows the entire balance to be drained by the second call.

For any admissible call to the fallback function, the contract's ETH balance should remain non-zero if and only if the block number is not a multiple of 15; the mutated version always retains all funds regardless of block number, violating the rule when block.number % 15 == 0.

After any successful fallback invocation, the contract should remain alive (i.e., have code at its address). The reference always preserves the contract, but when block.number % 15 == 0 the mutant selfdestructs it, violating this invariant.

After any successful fallback invocation with block.number % 15 == 0, the contract's self-balance should be zero. The reference sends the balance to the caller, fulfilling this; the mutant selfdestructs, transferring the balance but leaving the contract with no code instead, thus the test must check both conditions.

After any successful fallback invocation that does not revert, the contract C must have non-zero code size (remain alive). The mutant selfdestructs the contract when block.number % 15 == 0, violating this invariant.
After any successful fallback invocation, the contract C must have non-zero code size (remain alive). The mutant selfdestructs the contract when block.number % 15 == 0, violating this invariant.

After any successful fallback invocation, the contract's code size must remain non-zero (the contract stays alive). In the reference this always holds, but the mutant selfdestructs when block.number % 15 == 0, violating the invariant.

After every fallback call, the pastBlockTime must be strictly less than the block timestamp if it was set in a previous call; the buggy version sets pastBlockTime before the check, making the require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) always pass immediately after the assignment in the same call.

After two successful fallback calls, pastBlockTime must strictly increase from the first call's timestamp to the second call's timestamp; the buggy version sets pastBlockTime before the check, causing the second call's pastBlockTime to equal its own timestamp instead of the previous one's, violating strict inequality.

After a successful fallback call, pastBlockTime must equal the block.timestamp of that transaction; the buggy version sets pastBlockTime before the check so the require never fails, but pastBlockTime is still the current block.timestamp, so the assertion itself won't catch the difference — instead, the bug changes the revert behavior: the original reverts on a call with block.timestamp <= pastBlockTime, but the mutant never reverts due to the timestamp check because it assigns pastBlockTime first, making the check always pass within the same call.
A fallback call that should revert because block.timestamp is not strictly greater than a pastBlockTime that was set in the SAME block by a prior fallback call will incorrectly succeed in the mutant.
